11083-the-parables-of-the-saviour-the-go:
The tenth book of the Good Child's Library presents the parables of Jesus in easy verse, with brilliant illuminations from original designs, published in 1851. The publishers aimed to encourage scripture reading by giving children the most interesting New Testament stories in attractive verse, with pictures printed in oil colours, a costly process they pioneered in America.

Fourteen parables follow, from the Sower and the Tares and the Wheat to the Good Samaritan, the Prodigal Son, the Ten Virgins, and the Judgment. The Barren Fig Tree verses warn that grace refused will not last forever, while the Unjust Judge urges prayer without fainting. The book suits family reading and Sunday schools, teaching Bible stories through rhyme and colour.
11174-four-great-americans-washington-fr:
James Baldwin wrote this schoolroom biography for young Americans, telling four lives in short, plain chapters. Washington the surveyor and general, Franklin the printer and inventor, Webster the orator, and Lincoln the backwoods lawyer turned president. Each life is broken into episodes a child could follow, from Washington's boyhood to Franklin's kite experiment and Lincoln's years in Illinois.

The book's aim is character teaching as much as history, presenting hard work, honesty, and persistence as the thread joining its subjects. Anecdotes carry most of the argument, with battles and politics kept in the background. It still works as an introduction to four figures American schools long treated as models.
11251-famous-reviews-selected-and-edited:
This large anthology collects famous critical reviews with introductory notes, sampling how leading writers judged new books across the nineteenth century and beyond. Reviewers praise, scold, and anatomize novels, poems, and histories, and the editor's notes place each review in its quarrel or moment. The result is less a history of literature than a history of literary opinion.

For students, the volume's value is comparative: the same kinds of praise and blame recur, aimed at very different books. It shows criticism as a public act, shaping reputations in real time. Readers who enjoy literary argument will find the collection's combativeness its main pleasure.
12336-brown-wolf-and-other-jack-london-s:
Franklin K. Mathiews, chief Scout librarian of the Boy Scouts of America, chose this Jack London story collection for young readers. The table of contents runs from Brown Wolf and That Spot through Trust, All Gold Canyon, The Story of Keesh, and The Heathen.

Brown Wolf opens with a woman delaying for dew-wet grass to put on overshoes, then finding a stray dog at her door. Other stories follow gold hunters, Eskimo boys, and sailors, with London usual themes of loyalty, endurance, and the wild. A mid-book tale has Koogah reprove a boaster for notching his stick too coarsely. Mathiews selection softens London harshest work for scouts, but keeps his vigor. The book introduced generations of boys to London.
14630-ruth-fielding-on-cliff-island-or-t:
Alice B. Emerson's Ruth Fielding on Cliff Island, subtitled The Old Hunter's Treasure Box, sends Ruth and her school friends to an island adventure. Cupples and Leon published the illustrated volume in 1915.

Ann flings a rope across a pond to Heavy, the plump girl, while a young fellow wraps the slack round a sapling and urges easy pulling, lest they drag the boat. Treasure hunting, boating, and camp fun follow. The book is a lively girls' series tale, in the Ruth Fielding line, with pluck, friendship, and a mystery at its center.
17498-when-knighthood-was-in-flower-or-t:
Charles Major's Tudor romance, presented as the memoir of Sir Edwin Caskoden, tells the love story of Charles Brandon and the Princess Mary. Chapters run from the Caskodens and a duel to Brandon's coming to court. A lesson in dancing follows, then an honour that makes an enemy, a rare ride to Windsor, and love's fierce sweetness. Trouble in Billingsgate Ward and a warning not to put trust in princesses darken the later pages.

Set in the court of Henry the eighth, the novel mixes history with romance, giving Brandon's rise and his daring love a swashbuckling frame. Readers get one of the most popular American historical romances of its era, full of court intrigue, swordplay, and royal favour. Its charm lies in its brisk pace and its fondness for Tudor colour.
18482-the-most-ancient-lives-of-saint-pa:
Rev. James O'Leary edited this volume of the most ancient lives of Saint Patrick, including the life by Jocelin, hitherto unpublished in America, with Patrick's extant writings. The fifth edition appeared in New York from P. J. Kenedy in 1880, entered for copyright in 1874. A frontispiece shows Saints Columba, Patrick, and Brigida from an engraving made at Paris in 1629.

The lives open with Calphurnius, son of Potitus, a Briton presbyter living near the Irish Sea, who married Conchessa, niece of Martin of Tours. From that family Patrick's story grows, through captivity, calling, and mission to Ireland. A preface and chronological table guide readers through old texts. Readers get Patrick as his earliest biographers told him: apostle, wonder worker, and founder, in lives written centuries after his death.
19144-report-by-the-governor-on-a-visit-:
This 1908 colonial report by the Governor of Newfoundland covers a visit to the Micmac Indians at Bay d'Espoir. Presented to Parliament, it prints the governor's letter, photographs by James Howley, and extracts from official records. The report costs two pence and bears the number fifty-four.

Micmacs, a branch of Algonquins from Maine, New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia, reached Newfoundland about a century before, after Beothuks, who had held the land without firearms, were nearly destroyed. A proclamation of 1810 threatened death for murdering a Beothuk. Readers get a short, official ethnographic record of its era.
19155-the-seminole-indians-of-florida-fi:
Clay MacCauley wrote this Smithsonian report on the Seminole Indians of Florida, printed as part of the Bureau of Ethnology's fifth annual report. It describes a small, hard-pressed people after wars with the United States, counting only just over two hundred souls in Florida at the time. Tables break the count by age.

Chapters cover dress, hair, beads, silver disks, homes, food, and social custom, with care for both men and women. MacCauley notes health, climate, and habits as causes of growth or loss. Readers get a detailed ethnographic record, valuable yet framed by the views of its era.
21279-2-b-r-0-2-b:
Kurt Vonnegut Jr. published this short story in Worlds of If in January 1962, taking its title from Hamlet's question, spelled out in digits and letters. Everything is perfectly swell in its future: no prisons, slums, poverty, or wars. All diseases are conquered, and so is old age.

Death, barring accidents, is an adventure for volunteers, and America's population is held at forty million. In a Chicago lying-in hospital, Edward K. Wehling Jr., fifty-six and young by the age's standards, waits for his wife to bear triplets. In this world, new life requires room. The title gives the way out, and the story turns on who must take it.
22037-the-life-public-services-and-selec:
Rutherford B. Hayes rose from Civil War general to Governor of Ohio and then President. Campaign lives like this one introduced such a candidate to the voters. The book traces the Hayes line back to George Hayes of Scotland, who settled at Windsor, Connecticut, in 1682. From that stock, it argues, came a fitting Republican candidate for President.

Family history gives way to war service, Congress, and the governorship. A generous share of the volume prints Hayes's own speeches, so readers could judge his words directly. Such books were tools of persuasion as much as records. This one preserves the image of Hayes that his party carried into the disputed election of 1876.
24639-the-colonial-mortuary-bard-reo-the:
Louis Becke published these three South Seas pieces with T. Fisher Unwin in 1901. The first takes its title from a writer in the Sydney Evening News, who printed amusing entries from a visitors' book at Longwood on St. Helena, where Napoleon died. Becke compares them with mortuary verse from a Melbourne newspaper.

One Melbourne epitaph tells how angels envied fair Emily and whispered they would take her away on Tuesday night. Becke once thought it the noblest mortuary verse ever written, then changed his mind. The companion pieces follow Reo the fisherman and the black bream of Australia, giving readers Becke's wry, salty view of colonial life.
25511-ballads-of-mystery-and-miracle-and:
Frank Sidgwick selects and edits this second series of Popular Ballads of the Olden Time, published in London in 1904. Mystery and miracle supply the first half, with Thomas Rymer, Allison Gross, Tam Lin, the Wife of Usher's Well, and the Great Silkie of Sule Skerrie among the tales.

Fyttes of mirth follow, adding comic and lighter ballads to balance ghosts, fairies, and doomed lovers. The Three Ravens, the Twa Corbies, Young Benjie, and the Lyke-Wake Dirge appear among the later entries. Sidgwick prints the old texts with notes, aiming at a serviceable popular edition that general readers could trust and enjoy.
26021-sioux-indian-courts-an-address-del:
Doane Robinson of Pierre, South Dakota, tells the South Dakota Bar Association about Sioux Indian courts in an address of January 21, 1909. Robinson says the Sioux in their primitive life held an intelligent system of jurisprudence, varying by band as state court practice varies, yet resting on the same broad principles through the confederacy. His authorities were intelligent Sioux men, Hump, One Bull, Wakutemani, and Simon Kirk.

Robinson admits the difficulty of fixing the laws of an unlettered people who now live under conquerors' rules and must trust tradition for old ways. One tale shows a judiciary not wholly incorruptible: guests invited to a feast in a lodge ate their fill, smoked, and forgave a contempt of court. Modern Sioux courts, first proposed by General Harney in 1856 under federal law, get fuller treatment.
26572-chips-from-a-german-workshop-volum:
F. Max Müller published this third volume of Chips from a German Workshop at New York in 1871, gathering essays on literature, biography, and antiquities. Müller, a foreign member of the French Institute, writes as a bridge between German and English letters. He dedicates the book to Francis Turner Palgrave, who helped his first attempts at writing in English.

Essays cover German literature and old German love-songs, a life of Schiller, and Wilhelm Müller, the poet who died in 1827. Joinville, Shakespeare, Bacon in Germany, and a German traveller in England widen the view, while Cornish antiquities and letters from Bunsen, 1848 to 1859, close the volume. It suits readers curious about how German scholarship read the past.
27547-british-borneo-sketches-of-brunai-:
W. H. Treacher, secretary to the Government of Perak and first Governor of British North Borneo, wrote these sketches of Brunai, Sarawak, Labuan, and North Borneo. They were reprinted from the Journal of the Straits Settlements Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society, and printed at Singapore in 1891.

The first chapter runs from the Hudson's Bay Company's charter of 1670 to the British North Borneo Company's charter of November 1881. Treacher notes Friar Odoric in 1322, Portuguese and Spanish visits in 1518 and 1521, and Pigafetta's report of a Chinese trading community. Spanish attacks, Dutch and British connections, diamonds, and an East India Company factory follow. The sketches give a compact colonial history.
2939-william-harvey-and-the-discovery-of:
Thomas Henry Huxley lectured on William Harvey, the Englishman who discovered the circulation of the blood. Harvey was born in 1578 to a small Kent landowner, studied at Cambridge, and lived nearly to eighty, dying in 1657. His father sent the eldest son to university while the other sons went into trade and grew rich.

Huxley contrasts Harvey's account with Galen's older view, under which artery walls actively contracted and dilated like the heart, and the pulse resembled something other than a bag filled and emptied. Harvey showed the blood moves in a circuit, driven by the heart. The lecture honors a discoverer whose experiment overturned fifteen centuries of medical doctrine.
30980-kidnapped-at-the-altar-or-the-roma:
Laura Jean Libbey wrote this melodrama, billed as her new ten-thousand-dollar story, published by the Arthur Westbrook Company in Cleveland, Ohio, in 1909. Its heroine is Jessie Bain, saucy and much loved. Its chapters carry her from young girls finding love so sweet through fate against some people and the girl who plays at flirtation to the mysterious house on Wau-Winet Island.

Later chapters bring a mother's desperate scheme, Gerelda's escape from Wau-Winet Island, a collision with the pilot at the wheel, and love as a poisoned arrow in some hearts. They end with Jessie Bain entering the house of secrets. The closing chapters promise Hubert Varrick rescuing Jessie Bain, after chapters titled I Love Jessie with Heart and Soul and Hubert Cares for Me No Longer. It is a breathless romance of love, peril, and rescue.
31338-an-account-of-the-diseases-which-w:
Donald Monro's 1764 account, printed in London for Millar, Wilson, Durham, and Payne, records the diseases most frequent in British military hospitals in Germany. It covers January 1761 to the troops' return to England in March 1763. Monro, physician to the king's army and to St. George's Hospital, adds an essay on preserving soldiers' health and conducting military hospitals.

Dedicated to the king, whose inquiries into military hospitals in every quarter and concern for suffering officers and soldiers Monro praises, the book aims to ease miseries. Those miseries necessarily attend military life in service. It remains a foundational text of military medicine, grounded in wartime hospital experience.
32860-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, volume ten, runs alphabetically from Edwardes to Ehrenbreitstein. It opens with Sir Herbert Benjamin Edwardes, soldier-statesman in India, born at Frodesley in 1819, cadet of the East India Company in 1840, and writer for the Delhi Gazette.

Later entries cover Edwards, Eger, Egeria, Egerton, Egg, Egham, Edwardsville, Eglantine, Edwin king of Northumbria, Eglinton, Egmont, egoism, and eel. The longest article treats Egypt, its priesthood in four orders, its temples, and its dynasties, from Psammetichus, who recovered prosperity after Assyrian invasions, to the sack of Thebes. Each entry gives the concise, scholarly treatment of the eleventh edition.
35353-the-riverside-bulletin-march-1910-:
Houghton Mifflin lists its spring and summer books in The Riverside Bulletin for March 1910, from Park Street in Boston. A plate by James Montgomery Flagg from The Right Stuff heads the list. Prices are marked as open to change when each book comes out.

Fiction leads the list with The Duke's Price, by Demetra and Kenneth Brown, at one dollar and twenty cents net. Its heroine, the daughter of a New York multi-millionaire, weds a French duke and moves to his family château. The blurb stresses that this duke is no stock stage villain but a proud, sad gentleman. Praise for the wife is split with praise for him as strains grow. Demetra Vaka Brown won fame in 1909 for Haremlik, a study of Turkish women's lives.
36585-bahaism-and-its-claims-a-study-of-:
Samuel Graham Wilson, a missionary who lived thirty two years in Persia, published this study of the Baha'i faith with Fleming Revell in nineteen fifteen. Wilson writes as a controversialist examining a rival: the subtitle names it a study of the religion promulgated by Baha Ullah and Abdul Baha.

A sketch comes first, tracing the faith from Shi'a Islam through the Bab to Baha Ullah and his son Abdul Baha, whose tours of the West were then recent news. Later chapters set out the claims of the movement. A new religion is needed, Bahaism is that religion and means to supersede Christianity, and it will unify mankind under one language and one government. Wilson answers each claim from his mission station's vantage point. The book is a document of the missionary encounter with a world religion, detailed, hostile, and informed.
36646-the-philosophic-grammar-of-america:
Daniel Brinton, a professor of ethnology and archaeology in Philadelphia, set out Wilhelm von Humboldt's view of American languages. The book also holds Brinton's translation of an unpublished memoir by Humboldt on the American verb. Brinton led the Numismatic and Antiquarian Society of Philadelphia and sat in many learned bodies at home and abroad.

The work asks how language begins in the mind and how its roots and forms grow. Formal and material elements, and the development of languages, get close study. Humboldt held that the build of a tongue shows the mind of its people. For students of native American speech, the book links field facts to a grand theory of language itself.
39293-the-gentlemen-s-book-of-etiquette-:
Cecil B Hartley wrote The Gentlemen’s Book of Etiquette and Manual of Politeness for young men in society. G W Cottrell issued the book in Boston, with the copy filed in eighteen hundred sixty. Hartley drew on the best French, English, and American sources. The book bills itself as a full guide to a gentleman’s conduct.

Man was not made to live like a bear or a hermit, it opens. Each town, clique, and circle keeps its own forms and rites. The new man must learn them or jar at each step. Rules cover the street, the table, and the ball room. Morning calls and evening parties get their own full codes. Polite letters, dress, talk, and manly sports round out the course. A sage friend guides best, but a book must serve when none is near.
4-lincoln-s-gettysburg-address-given-nov:
On a Pennsylvania battlefield in November 1863, Abraham Lincoln spoke for barely two minutes. His Gettysburg Address dedicated a cemetery for soldiers killed in the Civil War. The speech opens by recalling a nation conceived in liberty and equality.

Lincoln argues the dead have already consecrated the ground beyond any words. The living must carry on their unfinished work so government of, by, and for the people survives. Brief as it is, the address reframed the war as a test of democracy itself. Schoolchildren still memorize its closing lines, and its words mark the cemetery it dedicated.
40454-frivolities-especially-addressed-t:
A story collection by Richard Marsh, published at London in 1899. James Bowden issued the volume. The subtitle addresses readers tired of being serious. Marsh also wrote Tom Ossington's Ghost and The Beetle. Review clippings in the front pages praise his ghost work warmly. Twelve tales fill the contents list.

The titles promise light mischief. A purse is found, and a burglar blunders. A honeymoon trip and a battlefield up to date appear. The first story opens at breakfast. A tall, seedy stranger calls about an advertised purse. He offers to pay the advertisement's cost for his property back. His vagueness about when he lost it smells wrong at once. Marsh spins comedy and mild mystery from such small hooks.
41704-the-religion-of-ancient-palestine-:
The Religion of Ancient Palestine in the second millennium before Christ is a study by Stanley Cook of Cambridge, issued at London in 1908. Cook was a lecturer in Hebrew and Syriac, and had written on Aramaic writings and on the laws of Moses beside Hammurabi's code. The subtitle promises his method: the faith of that land read in the light of digging and of inscriptions.

His contents move from sacred sites to sacred things, then to rites. The sanctuary at Gezer and other holy places open the survey. Trees, stones, images, and signs follow. Burial of the dead, jar burial, and the dark matter of human offering fill the rites chapter. The world of spirits, with awe, charms, and oracles, closes the visible list.
43345-the-other-world-or-glimpses-of-the:
The Other World, or Glimpses of the Supernatural, was edited by Frederick George Lee and published at London in 1875. Lee was vicar of All Saints at Lambeth when he made the set. Volume one of two presents facts, records, and traditions of the unseen. Dreams, omens, and miraculous occurrences lead the list of its topics.

Apparitions, wraiths, warnings, and second sight fill out the table of themes. Witchcraft and necromancy close the roll of subjects on the title page. A front essay asks whether one believes in prophecies and miracles at all. The answer given is yes and no, since much depends on the case in hand. Wonders of God are not to be tossed aside as fables without a hearing, the editor argues.
43346-the-other-world-or-glimpses-of-the:
The Other World, or Glimpses of the Supernatural is the next part of a two part set, out in eighteen seventy-five. The Reverend Frederick George Lee, a church man of London, shaped the set. It holds facts, notes, and old tales of dreams, signs, ghosts, wraiths, and the sight of things to come. A quote from the book of Job heads the first part here.

Parts treat ghosts of men at the point of death, houses and spots that ghosts haunt, and the new cult of calls to the dead. That cult takes two parts of this book. A sum and close end the work, with a full guide to names past the whole. One case tells of a slain girl whose ghost came past to name her slayer, a tale of the past age but two.
45143-the-way-to-the-west-and-the-lives-:
The Way to the West, by Emerson Hough, tells how America moved west, in three lives. Grosset and Dunlap issued the book in New York, from a copyright of 1903. Frederic Remington illustrated it, and Red River carts front it.

Four books chart the road: across the Alleghanies, to the Rockies, to the Pacific, and across it. The first book treats the tools first, before the men. The American ax, the rifle, the boat, and the horse each get a chapter. Then come the waters, the Mississippi, and the origin of the pioneer. Daniel Boone fills a chapter of that book. Davy Crockett leads the second, and Kit Carson the third, with the Santa Fé and Oregon trails. A divider marks 1834, when beaver trapping stopped paying. Iron trails and pathways of the future close it.
45531-narrative-of-the-life-and-travels-:
The Narrative of the Life and Travels of Serjeant B was written by the serjeant himself. It was printed at Edinburgh in eighteen twenty-three. The preface explains that the book began as a private journal. In it he kept an exact record of the providences that befell him.

Friends who heard the journal read pressed him to shape its best passages into a narrative. A clergyman under whose care he sat urged the work on warmly. The narrative follows his soldier's life and travels, including service connected with India. It frames escapes and hardships with the psalm texts on its title page. One reads: I shall not die, but live, and declare the works of the Lord. Such ranker's memoirs are rare, since most soldiers of his station never reached print.
46636-the-three-days-tournament-a-study-:
The Three Days' Tournament studies romance and folk lore. The book forms Number Fifteen of the Grimm Library. It stands as a supplement to the Lancelot study. That study was Number Twelve of the same line. A list of the line's books fronts this one. Prices and page counts fill the list.

Georgian folk tales in Marjory Wardrop's English open the list. The Legend of Perseus takes three volumes there. Edwin Sidney Hartland wrote that long study. The Voyage of Bran fills two more. Kuno Meyer edited that Irish saga text. Alfred Nutt added essays to both Bran volumes. Jessie L Weston's Gawain study stands in the line too. Cheap crown volumes like these put hard folk-lore learning into the hands of common readers in the 1900s.
47581-birds-and-all-nature-vol-4-no-3-se:
Birds and All Nature, volume 4, number 3, for September 1898, is a monthly magazine pictured by color photography. Its pages run from page 81 to page 120, and its table of contents mixes birds, beasts, verse, and short notes. The issue opens with Some Animal Propensities, an essay on theft in the animal world.

That essay tells how hive-bees robbed a bumble-bee nest by coaxing, not force, until wasps came and the owners left for good. Robins, it adds, steal feathers and drive larger birds from feeding grounds. Other pieces treat the herring gull, useful birds of prey, the raccoon, wild birds in London, the red-shouldered hawk, the doves of Venice, butterflies, the fox, and the gray squirrel. Such magazines taught nature study to general readers before radio and film.
47582-the-adventures-of-captain-mago-or-:
Léon Cahun wrote The Adventures of Captain Mago, a Phoenician expedition set in the year 1000 before the Christian era. Ellen Frewer translated it from the French. Charles Scribner's Sons published it in New York in 1889, with pictures by Philippoteaux. The frontispiece shows the Queen of Sheba. Cahun aimed his book mainly at the young.

In his preface Cahun is candid about his method. The book claims no original or scientific research. Its fiction carries instruction: a picture of the world as it stood a thousand years before Christ. He says plain authority backs every statement about the period and about the Phoenicians in particular. A sea captain's voyage lets readers meet the peoples, goods, and wonders of the ancient world in story form. The novel belongs to a nineteenth-century kind that taught history through adventure, dressing real scholarship in the clothes of a tale.
47610-sir-joshua-reynolds-discourses-edi:
The Discourses of Sir Joshua Reynolds are talks on the art of paint. Reynolds gave them as the head of the king's school of art. Helen Zimmern shaped this set, out in London in 1887. The first talk tells what good the school does for the craft.

It bids the young heed the rules of art with full trust at first. It bids the chiefs check a rush to a loose, swift hand in the young. Hard work must be urged at all times, the talk holds. That work must be aimed at the right marks in the art. The next talk maps the course and the steps of the craft. It warns that much mere copy work starves the young hand. The talks then rise to the grand style and its chief laws.
48085-birds-and-all-nature-vol-6-no-2-se:
Birds and All Nature, volume six, number two, is the September 1899 issue of a nature magazine illustrated by color photography. The number opens with The Pointer, a study of the sporting dog. That article weighs the old quarrel over the parent stock of domestic dogs: wolf, jackal, fox, or the wild dog of India. The writer argues that no single animal can claim the paternity of races so different in form and nature.

The contents range across the whole field of popular natural history. Shells and shell-fish, ores and minerals stand for the earth sciences. Mandioca, the water lily and awesome trees cover plants. Nature study in the public schools and the influence of pictures cover teaching. The yellow perch and the white swan close the animal roll.
48661-the-circle-of-knowledge-a-classifi:
The Circle of Knowledge is a one volume fact book issued in 1916, with a chief editor named Ruoff. Its subtitle promises essential facts of everyday interest across a vast range. Nature, geography, history, travel, and government stand first in that list. Science, invention, education, language, and writing follow close behind.

Fine arts, philosophy, religion, industry, and biography round out the sweep of the book. A bold line on the title page gives its aim in three short claims. The book is easy to read, easy to grasp, and easy to retain, it says. Ruoff had edited other fact books before this one, and they are listed here. The work sorts its store of facts into classes so a reader can find a topic fast.
48704-autobiography-of-matthew-scott-jum:
Autobiography of Matthew Scott, Jumbo's Keeper pairs Scott's life story with his biography of the elephant Jumbo. It was printed at Bridgeport, Connecticut, in 1885. Scott had kept animals at the London Zoological Gardens, and the Society's medal of 1866 honoured his success in breeding foreign animals.

Scott dedicates the book, in January 1885, to the people of the United States and Great Britain. He thanks both countries for kindness received in his travels with Jumbo. His first chapter promises a humble and truthful record, written for the enlightenment of fellow men. He was born at Knowsley, in Lancashire, England, in 1834, and he begins there with his start in life.
49048-two-centuries-of-new-milford-conne:
Two Centuries of New Milford, Connecticut records the bicentennial celebration of the founding of the town, held June 15 to 18, 1907. The Grafton Press published the book in New York the same year, in an edition of one thousand copies. A portrait of Roger Sherman, the town's most famous son, from a painting by Ralph Earle, opens the volume.

Historical articles and reminiscences, prepared under a town historical committee, fill the book. An introduction treats the first settlers, the organizing of the township and the church, and the sturdy character of the fathers. Glimpses of old New Milford follow: the first meetinghouse, seating and dignifying it, people called to church by a drum, and the tithing-man. Churches, schools, singing schools, and the early wars all get their due. The book is a town's memory of itself at two hundred years.
49265-the-sisters-of-lady-jane-grey-and-:
Sisters of Lady Jane Grey is a Tudor history by Richard Davey. Davey also wrote The Sultan and His Subjects and The Pageant of London. A front plate shows Lady Katherine Grey from an unknown artist's painting. Her motto verse likens her fate to a flower that withers in an hour. The subtitle names Charles Brandon, duke of Suffolk, as wicked grandfather.

True stories tell the strange lives of Katherine and of Mary Grey. Their sister Jane reigned nine days as queen before her fall. Brandon's marriages and ambitions set the sisters' peril in train at court. Tudor succession plots, secret weddings, and royal wrath fill their short lives. Davey writes popular history with a storyteller's eye for pathos and colour.
49797-book-of-american-baking-a-practica:
The Book of American Baking is a trade manual for professional bakers, published by the American Trade Publishing Company of New York in 1910. Its full title promises a practical guide to several branches of the industry. Cakes, buns, and pastry share the cover with bread making and pie baking.

Four parts divide the contents. Cakes, buns, and pastry come first, then pie baking, then bread making. A miscellaneous part sweeps up the rest of the bakeshop. The index begins with a recipe called Alberts. Subscribers to Bakers Weekly could write in for any recipe the book lacked, free of charge. The manual served working bakers rather than home cooks. Its formulas are scaled and phrased for the trade, a snapshot of the American bakery just before the great chain bakeries rose.
50115-struggles-and-triumphs-or-forty-ye:
Struggles and Triumphs is the autobiography of Phineas Barnum, the great American showman, in the author's edition of 1872. Its sub-title calls it forty years' recollections, and the life runs complete to April of that year. Barnum opens with a card to the public on the book's vast sale. The cloth book had sold at three dollars and a half and up, a rare run for its day. He dedicates the tale to his wife and family. Its motto calls the book a map of busy life.

In his preface Barnum claims a career crowded past most men's. Success and defeat take their turns through the tale. He travelled widely at home and abroad, and knew the humble and the famed. He held, he says, the first place among those who gave the American people sound amusement.
50389-autobiography-of-samuel-s-hildebra:
The Autobiography of Samuel Hildebrand presents the confession of the renowned Missouri bushwhacker. It was taken down in 1870 and backed by sworn statements of its truth. Wendell Keith certifies that Hildebrand, whom he had known from boyhood, came to his house at Big River Mills in January 1870. There Hildebrand dictated his whole war record. Keith wrote it out and then compiled it with James Evans, and neighbors of Ste. Genevieve County swore before a notary that the account was genuine.

Hildebrand rode with the guerrilla war that tore Missouri apart during the Civil War. His narrative gives that border conflict from the bushwhacker's side: the raids, the pursuits, and the killings that made his name feared. Books of this kind sold confession and adventure together. Whatever a reader discounts for self-defense, the autobiography is a raw primary voice from Missouri's guerrilla war.
51683-the-surprising-and-singular-advent:
The Surprising and Singular Adventures of a Hen was related by the hen herself to her family of chickens. Whittingham and Arliss published it at the Juvenile Library in Paternoster Row, London, in eighteen fifteen. The tale opens on a kind farm in the vale of Ravensworth. Its owners treat all their animals with humanity, the yard is large and clean, and a clear brook at its foot entertains ducks and geese.

A chick runs to her speckled mother with a demand for revenge. A nasty young bantam cock stole the fine fat worm she had just scratched up and crowed over. The mother refuses to kill anyone before hearing the offence, then agrees to tell her own story instead. In the laburnum's shade she will relate the chief events of her eventful life, and the children's book becomes a hen's memoir.
52569-the-bondage-and-travels-of-johann-:
A captive's tale fills this volume: The Bondage and Travels of Johann Schiltberger, a native of Bavaria, in Europe, Asia, and Africa from 1396 to 1427. It was rendered from a Heidelberg manuscript edited in 1859 by Neumann, and printed at London in 1879 for a society that publishes old voyages. The translator was a naval commander, Telfer, with notes by a professor at Odessa.

A Latin dedication gives the narrative to a German crown prince, as a witness of duty, calling it the tale of the most wretched fortunes of a Bavarian soldier. Lists of the society's council follow. The rendering carries the old soldier's own account of capture and long wandering, first printed from his manuscript. The translator's preface, introduction, and notes go with it, and the notes of Bruun besides, and a map.
52991-waterloo-days-the-narrative-of-an-:
Charlotte A Eaton remembers June 1815 in Waterloo Days, the narrative of an Englishwoman resident at Brussels in June 1815. George Bell and Sons of London issued this new edition in 1888. Edward Bell adds an introduction and appendix. The little book was first published within two years of the events it describes.

Bell's introduction tells who she was: Charlotte Anne Waldie, born in 1788, who came to Brussels with her brother and younger sister as Wellington's headquarters gathered. Her account of those momentous days, revised in 1852 as The Days of Battle, is called graphic and interesting. Eyewitness history stands here.
54626-being-a-summary-statement-of-the-i:
Arthur Beeley wrote the summary statement on the Mormon question in England. The Millennial Star office at Liverpool printed and published it. Its office stood at 295 Edge Lane in that city. The subject is an investigation made by the British government. Beeley opens on the sensational press and its daily captions against his church.

Beware of the Mormons, one caption runs in his list of horrors. Capturing soul-brides for Utah, another headline charges the elders. Local girl kidnapped by a Mormon, a third caption cries. The elder is painted a villain of the deepest dye, he writes. White-slave traffic and the basest practices stand charged against him. Strange to say, Christian ministers instigate many of these charges, he adds. Let an impartial tribunal judge, he answers the man in the street. Professor Anson on the Home Secretary's duties stands in his argument.
55350-counterfeit-money-the-green-goods-:
Counterfeit Money: The Green Goods Business Exposed for the Benefit of All who have Dishonest Inclinations is number twenty two of the Multum in Parvo Library. It is dated Boston, October 1895, and calls itself the smallest magazine in the world. Single copies cost five cents.

Facts about the green goods business, the text opens. Every good thing has its imitation, and this includes money. Counterfeiting dates back to old Greek and Roman times. The despicable business has been kept up ever since, and probably always will be. In some countries, conviction for making or passing spurious coin means death. Yet people of dishonest tendencies have a mania for wanting to shove the queer. Readers get a penny exposé of the classic counterfeit swindle.
55548-fifty-years-of-freedom-with-matter:
Fifty Years of Freedom is an address by the Reverend Francis Grimke, given in October 1913. He spoke first in Baltimore, then at the Fifteenth Street Presbyterian Church in Washington. The title page adds that it treats matters of vital importance to both the white and coloured people of the United States. Verses on liberty stand at its head. The fifty years are those since emancipation. Grimke is careful on the date: the proclamation freed no one while the war ran.

Freedom came in fact, he says, with Lee's surrender at Appomattox in April 1865. Grant's victorious army gave the paper its force. Fifty years is a long span in a man's life, he grants, but a short one in the life of a race. It is long enough to pause and take stock. Grimke weighs what his people have gained, and what wrongs stand undone.
55789-list-of-books-in-belles-lettres-pu:
John Lane, The Bodley Head, of Vigo Street, London, issued a Catalogue of Publications in Belles Lettres in eighteen ninety five, all at net prices. A note states the terms. Authors and publisher reserve the right of reprinting any book in the list if a new edition is called for, it says. Most books appear simultaneously in England and America, it adds. Entries run by author in alphabetical order.

Francis Adams Essays in Modernity, crown octavo at five shillings net, stands near the front, with Stone and Kimball of Chicago as American house. Grant Allen The Lower Slopes, a volume of verse in six hundred copies, follows. The Woman Who Did is sent to the Keynotes Series, it notes. Aubrey Beardsley Story of Venus and Tannhäuser appears in the list. Book historians get a famed fin de siècle publisher list, with prices and formats.
56021-poisonous-snakes-of-texas-and-firs:
Poisonous Snakes of Texas and First Aid Treatment of Their Bites is a state bulletin. John Werler, director of the Houston Zoological Gardens, wrote the guide. The Texas Parks and Wildlife Department issued it at Austin, Texas. Bulletin number 31 first came out in February of 1950. Revisions and reprints ran through 1952, 1963, and on to 1970.

Hunters, ranchers, telephone crews, and Boy Scouts asked for the guide. Sixteen species and subspecies of poisonous snakes live in Texas. Pit vipers open the kinds: copperheads in four forms stand first. The western cottonmouth follows, then rattlesnakes in nine listed forms. Western diamondback, timber, canebrake, and Mojave stand among those rattlers. The Texas coral snake closes the kinds as the elapid entry. Venoms, diagnosing the bite, and first aid fill the closing parts. Suggestions to physicians end the practical bulletin for field folk.
56540-miss-parloa-s-young-housekeeper-de:
Maria Parloa published Miss Parloa's Young Housekeeper at Boston in 1894, designed especially to aid beginners. Parloa founded two schools of cookery and wrote the Appledore Cook Book and a kitchen companion. The book offers economical receipts for those cooking for two or three.

Her preface says fifteen years of teaching brought earnest appeals for a book aimed at those just beginning to keep house. Young wives wanted to know how to buy supplies for a small family and how to cook economically. Readers get a famous cooking teacher scaling her art down to the smallest household, where waste hurts most and portions are hardest to judge.
56926-robin-hood-a-collection-of-all-the:
Joseph Ritson gathered all the ancient poems, songs, and ballads then extant about Robin Hood, the celebrated English outlaw. This large paper edition, printed at London in 1885 in one hundred numbered copies, follows Ritson's own annotated edition of 1795. Historical anecdotes of Robin's life stand before the ballads themselves.

Thomas Bewick cut eighty wood engravings for the book, printed here on China paper, and nine etchings from new paintings are added. The first part opens with the long Lytell Geste of Robyn Hode, then Robin and the potter, the beggar, and Guy of Gisborne. The second part turns to Robin's birth, breeding, valour, and marriage, and his progress to Nottingham.
60759-the-englishman-s-house-a-practical:
Richardson wrote The Englishman's House, a practical guide for selecting or building a house, in a third edition with nearly six hundred drawings. Richardson had written on old English mansions and on the warming of buildings. His preface says the volume holds plans for cottages, villas, and small and large mansions. Most of the plans, he notes, have been built in fact.

Numbered designs run from a gardener's cottage and a village Sunday school to park lodges and a sculptor's villa. A part on concrete construction for cottages sits among the early designs. Later parts treat foundations, damp, and fireproof building, and a long part treats the fireplace. A lecture hall, stabling, and a bachelor's house widen the range for the home builder.
61854-the-runaway-equator-and-the-strang:
The Runaway Equator is a children's fantasy by Lilian Bell, published in New York in 1911. Peter Newell drew its pictures. A frontispiece shows the Equator making off, a mile or two away. The first chapter brings Billy together with Nimbus. An enchanted trolley car follows, and then the news: the Equator is loose.

Billy pursues it past the equine ox and the evening star. He climbs a passive volcano, meets Jack Frost, and follows the runaway's trail. One chapter lands where night is six months long. The chase ends twelve chapters in. Bell turns geography into nonsense adventure in the manner young readers loved.
63057-ruins-of-buddhistic-temples-in-pra:
Ruins of Buddhistic Temples in Praga Valley is an archaeological study by Doctor Groneman, translated from the Dutch and printed at Semarang in Java in 1912. Its subject is the great Buddhist monuments of central Java: the temples of Borobudur, Mendut, and Pawon. Groneman had settled near Yogyakarta to study the antiquities at first hand.

His preface tells the circumstances. Sickness forced him to retire from medical practice in 1896. He returned to Yogyakarta to devote himself to the antiquarian and ethnological studies he loved, living near the chief Hindu ruins of the Parambanan plain and the Praga valley. He complains that the government does not assist such work. Much, he says, remains unexplained in the sculpture and symbolism of these images, and some have been wrongly understood. The book is his remedy.
64231-buffalo-bill-and-the-overland-trai:
Buffalo Bill and the Overland Trail is a boys' historical novel by Edwin Sabin, published by Lippincott in 1914 in the American Trail Blazers series. The series promised vivid fiction on accurate fact: the story grips and the history sticks. Sabin's subject is William Cody, from pony express boy to the world-famed Buffalo Bill.

The story is told through Davy, a boy who joins the wagon trains and meets Billy Cody by the way. Chapters follow the trail trades in order: freight wagons, gold fever, and the pony express. Sabin dedicates the book to the old plains freighters, plodding at three miles an hour across a thousand hostile miles. It is frontier history recast as a boy's apprenticeship.
65196-floral-illustrations-of-the-season:
Floral Illustrations of the Seasons is a flower book of 1831, printed in London from drawings by Mrs Edward Roscoe of Liverpool. Its full title promises the most beautiful, hardy, and rare plants of the flower garden. The plates were engraved by R. Havell the younger. The work is dedicated to William Roscoe, the author's father, in a letter dated March 1829. Her preface speaks with modesty of her aim. She hopes to set the plants in a fair form, with true and useful notes.

She wishes most of all to stir a taste for botany among her own sex. A garden, she quotes, is among the purest of human joys. In the build of each plant she finds fine order and wise contrivance. The plates run with the seasons, as the title says.
6588-types-of-children-s-literature-a-co:
Walter Barnes gathers the world's best writing for children into one volume for use in colleges, normal schools, and library schools. The aim, as the publisher states it, is to put knowledge to work for children's needs, and to guide parents and teachers through a vast, rich field. Specimens of each kind of children's writing appear for study and for reading aloud.

Fairy tales, fables, poems, and stories sit side by side, each chosen to show its type at its best. Barnes adds notes to help older readers judge what suits a child and why. Types of Children's Literature is a useful, old-style course book, and a fine shelf of samples for any lover of children's books.
66750-nick-carter-stories-no-136-april-1:
Street and Smith issued a Nick Carter weekly dated April 17, 1915, at a price of five cents. The tale, named The Man They Held Back, casts Nick in masked dress for a ball. A costumer has sent the wrong garb, a Mexican rig with split trousers and a big sombrero in place of a Spanish officers dress.

Nick grumbles, but the mask may yet hide him from a gang of coin fakes he hunts. His aide Chick backs him, in talk that shows how well the pair know each trap and ruse. False coin, false dress, and a false face set up a swift dime tale of wits.
67247-the-real-question-as-to-altar-ligh:
Edward Phipps, rector of Stansfield, wrote a letter in October 1865 to a fellow clergyman on altar lights. It was printed at London that year. The letter answers a clash with the Bishop of Ely. The bishop had blanked a church where lights stood on the altar.

Phipps lays out the facts as he has them. The bishop came to hold a confirmation and lodged at the vicar's house. Hearing of the lights, he stayed away from the communion. A legal view was sent that called the lights unlawful. The bishop then moved his visitation to a church where daily prayer, Phipps notes, is wholly left unsaid.
716-the-cruise-of-the-jasper-b:
Don Marquis wrote this light adventure about Clement Cleggett, a New York newspaper man who buys a schooner, the Jasper B, and sails into romance. A bright blade, a skull, and a set of oblong boxes hint at piracy, lost treasure, and old scores. Lady Agatha, in distress, and the villain Logan Black cross his path.

Cleggett stands by his ship through storms, duels, and night raids, while wit and repartee fly as fast as cutlasses. Marquis mixes farce with swashbuckling, and the newspaper man's dry voice keeps the wild plot fun. The book is pure escapist fare, a comic sea romance for readers who like their adventure with a smile.
77113-the-autobiography-of-sir-henry-mor:
The Autobiography of Sir Henry Morton Stanley is kept here in its fourth edition, published in London by Sampson Low, Marston. Dorothy Stanley, his wife, edited the book, which carries sixteen illustrations, a map, and one facsimile letter. A title page crowds his honours: geographical gold medals from London, Paris, Italy, Sweden, and Antwerp, and grand cordons of half a dozen orders.

The editor's preface, dated from a Christmas 1914 printing, explains the book's making. Stanley left the autobiography unfinished at his death; his widow gives it to the world as he wished, filled out with full extracts from his journals, letters, and private note-books. His own letter of November 30, 1893, stands as introduction: he wanted a rough draft of his life, for the world knew his African work only as it touched those he served. The inner existence, the me, nobody knew.
britannica-1911-b:
B is the second letter of the alphabet. It matches the second symbol of the Phoenician alphabet. It keeps that place in all European alphabets except those drawn from medieval Greek, like Russian. In Greek the old symbol's sound had shifted from b to v, so Slavonic tongues had to invent a fresh sign for the true b sound.

Early forms of the letter looked like nines, and Greek lands reshaped it oddly: upside down at Thera, open-topped elsewhere, almost a C in some Ionic islands. The entry also fixes the sound itself in speech terms. It is a voiced stop made by closing the lips and sounding the voice. It differs from p by that voice. It differs from m by the closed nose passage. Letter shape and lip sound fill its pages.
brown-wolf-and-other-jack-london-stories:
Franklin K. Mathiews picked and edited a set of Jack London tales for young readers. Mathiews served as Chief Scout Librarian of the Boy Scouts of America. Twelve tales line the contents page. Brown Wolf gives the book its name and its first place.

That Spot, Trust, and All Gold Canyon follow. The Story of Keesh and Nam-Bok the Unveracious bring the far north in. Yellow Handkerchief, Make Westing, and The Heathen sail south seas ground. The Hobo and the Fairy, Just Meat, and A Nose for the King close the list. Brown Wolf opens in an orchard home. Walt Irvine and his wife hunt their run-off dog Wolf through wet grass and manzanita. Dog, wild, and tame pull form the knot of that first tale, and of much London work for boys.
doe-osti-17019151-synthesis-and-consolid:
Alex Avalos, Luke Van Buuren, Christian Bustillos, and colleagues at Lawrence Livermore tested two ceramics that might breed tritium inside a future fusion plant. Their September 2026 report compares lithium silicate, Li4SiO4, and lithium zirconate, Li2ZrO3. Fusion fuel tritium is scarce and short lived, so a plant must make its own supply in place.

Both materials were made from lithium carbonate plus oxide nanopowders, then fired and bent in ring on ring strength tests. Several silicate samples met both the strength and density thresholds set for the job. No zirconate sample met both at once, even as firing heat rose, so the authors judge it a poor choice on this early data.
doe-osti-17030340-fy26-final-report-238p:
Final fiscal year 2026 report from Los Alamos National Laboratory, issued September 29, 2026, presents a faster way to measure plutonium 238 in bulk environmental samples. Kimberly Hinrichs and eight colleagues adapted a mass spectrometry method, shortened to TIMS, so one chemistry pass yields all plutonium isotopes at once. The work supports the IAEA network of labs that analyze safeguard samples.

Sediment results matched certified values, and swipe sample ratios matched the older alpha counting method on identical copies. The new route gave better precision per sample and a detection limit about as low as alpha counting. One planned sample set, IAEA-385, was not analyzed because the project started about two months late.
doe-osti-2583501-fire-resistance-develop:
CRADA final report NREL/TP-2C00-94177, dated March 13, 2025, brings fire modeling to roofing. Nicholas Wimer was NREL's contact; the partner was a company called The R&D Lab. The UL 790 Class A burning brand test judges whether a roof covering resists severe external fire, essentially a burning brand laid on the roof. Running the real test again and again while developing new materials is slow and expensive.

The project replaced some of those burns with computation. NREL wrote a Python model of heat transfer from a Class A burning brand through the roof's resistive layers, shingle and underlayment, down to the wood deck. The partner ran instrumented test decks through actual burning brand tests, generating the data to validate and calibrate the model. With a trusted simulation, a designer can iterate on materials at a keyboard and reserve the costly certification test for designs already likely to pass.
doe-osti-2997168-solar-spectrum-conversi:
A cooperative project final report dated 30 September 2025, led at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory by Emory Chan with partner Mvmnt-X, covers light-converting coatings for algae growing systems. Algae use blue and red light for photosynthesis but waste much of the sun's near-infrared. The project built nanoparticles that absorb that infrared and re-emit it as visible light.

The winning particle has a sodium yttrium fluoride core doped with 20 percent ytterbium and 2 percent erbium, wrapped in a 10 nanometer shell of the same host. It converted 980 nanometer light to visible light with a quantum yield of 3.2 percent, measured under the project's stated test conditions. Clear films made from the particles kept strong optical quality. Robotic synthesis and computer modeling sped the search. Coatings of this kind could raise algae growth rates in biofuel reactors.
doe-osti-2997302-exploring-multilayer-ne:
Sandia National Laboratories final report SAND2025-12012R, by Eric Wallace, Mathias Boggs, Samuel Gailliot, and Adam Williams, tests whether layered network models can ground the strategy of integrated deterrence in measurable structure. Deterrence now spans military, economic, and diplomatic pressure at once. A multilayer network holds one layer per arena, with links inside and between them.

The team reviewed how escalation has been studied, then assembled data for the layers. United Nations ComTrade records fed the economic layer. Bilateral relationship data built the diplomatic layer, and an Asia Power Index fed comparisons of national strength. Functions combine the layers for analysis. Planners gain a test bed for asking how a move in one arena, say trade, propagates into the others before policy commits to it.
doe-osti-2997409-modular-autonomous-expe:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report LLNL-TR-2012130, by Diego Oyarzun Dinamarca with Aldair Gongora and Dante Ricci, dated October 2025, introduces a self-driving laboratory platform for biology. The full system, called MARS, links liquid-handling robots, robotic arms, and plate readers under one data system. Software chooses each next experiment from the last results, aiming to gain the most information per run.

This short version states the case plainly: manual work, long cycle times, and scattered data slow discovery in complex chemical and biological spaces. A modular, intelligent platform is offered as the fix, and as a model for future self-driving laboratories. The filing also frames the mission value for the laboratory: faster, more reliable campaigns that keep pace with modern experimental scale. Technical detail and test cases sit in the project's fuller reporting.
doe-osti-2997410-modular-autonomous-expe:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory full report LLNL-TR-2012135, by Diego Oyarzun Dinamarca, Aldair Gongora, and Dante Ricci, dated October 2025, documents the Modular Autonomous Research System, MARS. MARS joins laboratory robots, assorted instruments, and a central data system under artificial intelligence direction. Experiments run, data are read at once, and the next conditions are chosen to maximize what is learned.

Two main test cases proved the loop: metal-ligand binding assays read by spectroscopy, and peptide-directed mineralization, where peptides steer crystal growth. A dysprosium data set with the lamp-1 peptide shows how much readings can vary under identical conditions, the very noise the system must handle. Added testbeds cover electrochemistry for catalyst discovery and electrolyte mixing for advanced batteries. Campaigns ran with little human intervention, showing the platform's range.
doe-osti-3005839-total-column-infrared-t:
J. St. Clair of the University of Maryland, Baltimore County and NASA Goddard reports a deployment that produced no data, in ARM report DOE/SC-ARM-25-030, dated December 2025. The instrument was an EM27 infrared spectrometer, meant to measure total column amounts of trace gases over Baltimore from the ARM mobile facility. The original plan relied on a Morgan State undergraduate to run it through the summer.

When that staffing fell through, and no other funded team needed the instrument running, there was no urgency to make it operational. The results section states it plainly: no results were obtained. The deployment still taught the Goddard EM27 team lessons it will use at ten university sites in the coming year. Campaign reports that admit a null outcome keep the archive honest for everyone who searches it later.
doe-osti-3021706-thermal-compton-scatter:
Brookhaven National Laboratory technical note BNL-229489-2026-TECH, also numbered EIC-ADD-TN-159, by Andrii Natochii, dated February 2026, presents a Monte Carlo event generator for a subtle Electron-Ion Collider problem. The collider's electron beam constantly crosses the faint blackbody photon field inside the warm beam pipe. Occasionally an electron Compton-scatters off one of those thermal photons, loses energy, and leaves the beam, a slow drain on beam lifetime and a source of background.

The generator samples photon energies from the blackbody distribution and scatters electrons according to the Klein-Nishina cross section. To control computing cost, only electrons scattered beyond an energy deviation threshold of one part in a thousand are kept for tracking. Summing accepted events gives both the total Compton collision rate and the rate of electrons actually lost. The tool plugs into multi-turn tracking simulations of the collider.
doe-osti-3022050-a-guide-for-public-util:
A mini-guide by Hyleah O'Quinn helps state public utility commissions build the in-house technical skill that grid resilience work demands. It was prepared for the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners (NARUC), with support from the DOE Grid Deployment Office. It explains what resilience means in a regulatory setting. It also shows why staff who can judge engineering evidence matter when utilities propose resilience spending. And it lists the roles a commission needs, from power systems engineers to data analysts.

Practical hiring guidance follows. The guide sets out frameworks for defining resilience expertise. It then walks through hiring channels: graduate programs, energy firms, nearby technical fields such as civil engineering and meteorology, and mid-career changers. It closes with strategies for competing for scarce technical talent on public-sector pay, including partnerships, fellowships, and shared regional resources.
doe-osti-3024211-evaluating-energy-savin:
Paul Torcellini and Michael Young of the National Laboratory of the Rockies describe a hands-on way to judge building retrofit options, in report NLR/TP-5500-96097, dated March 2026. Instead of lecturing building teams about energy savings measures, the method runs as an interactive workshop where teams handle the choices themselves. Subject matter experts and support staff attend to answer questions about the technologies on the cards.

The report doubles as a facilitator's guide. Teams are told to tie their goals to their own organizational goals, or to Better Buildings goals they have already set. Roles and responsibilities for the expert facilitator are spelled out in bold, and key steps for each team are listed in order. The design aims at decisions a building owner can defend after the workshop ends.
doe-osti-3365798-implementation-of-a-hig:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-21371, by Jonathan C. Murray, implements a fast method for predicting the boundary layer on high-speed flight bodies of arbitrary shape. The boundary layer is the thin sheet of air dragged along a vehicle's skin; its state drives heating and drag at hypersonic speeds. Full simulations are costly, so an integral method that tracks layer averages offers a quick design tool.

The implementation builds on the MEIT integral model, adds a stagnation region treatment for the nose, and handles entrainment in curvilinear coordinates that follow curved bodies. Usage chapters cover reading CART3D flow solutions, solving, and extracting surface quantities and integrated loads. Wall states are among the outputs. Aerodynamicists get heating estimates early in design, before committing to heavyweight simulation.
doe-osti-3484473-radiolytic-gas-generati:
Argonne report ANL-26/35 studies gas buildup from radiolysis in a closed system holding molybdenum-99 solution. Sergey D. Chemerisov, Michael Kalensky, and Loren A. Knoblich are among the authors. Mo-99 is a medical isotope whose own radiation splits its solution into gas.

A piping diagram shows syringes, vacuum lines, filters, and shielded vials. Pressure sensors track gas as it forms in the product vial. Gas then moves to a shielded collection vial. Knowing pressure growth rates keeps shipping bottles safe. Isotope producers can size containers and relief paths with measured data.
famous-reviews-selected-and-edited-with-:
Johnson's Famous Reviews collects landmark book reviews from the great quarterlies. R. Brimley Johnson selected the pieces and added introductory notes. The London title page is dated 1914. A couplet from Pope on authors and critics fronts the contents.

The first section draws on the Edinburgh Review, founded in 1802. Lord Jeffrey appears on Southey's Thalaba and on Wordsworth's Excursion. Lord Brougham on Byron and Sydney Smith on Hannah More follow. Macaulay writes on Southey's Colloquies, Croker's Boswell, and Madame d'Arblay. Anonymous notices treat Wordsworth and Maturin's Melmoth. The Quarterly Review supplies the next section. Johnson frames reviewing as a literary art with its own masters and feuds.
four-great-americans-washington-franklin:
Baldwin tells four lives for young Americans: Washington, Franklin, Webster, and Lincoln. Each story begins in boyhood: Washington the surveyor, Franklin and his whistle, Webster the youngest son. The chapters stay short and plain, built for school readers.

Judge Ebenezer Webster explains where his money will go. He has land enough already, he tells a neighbor; he will try to educate his boys instead. Of his ten children the favorite was a black-haired little fellow called Daniel. James Baldwin, who also retold fifty famous stories, shaped these biographies as models of self-education and public service.
govdocs-archive_org-jfk-assassination-re:
In 2025 the United States government released a new wave of records on the assassination of President John F. Kennedy, under laws requiring the remaining files to come out. Batch two of that release gathers the documents as they were issued.

The papers run to memos, cables, and reports from the agencies that held Kennedy-era files, many of them previously redacted or withheld. Researchers read such batches slowly, comparing versions against earlier releases to find what changed. The file preserves the batch as a public record, complete as issued, for exactly that work.
govdocs-archive_org-national-socialist-a:
The National Socialist Anthology collects writings on the history and works of Heinrich Himmler and certain members of the SS. Its dedication is to Himmler himself, as Reichsführer-SS, which tells the reader plainly where the volume stands.

The anthology presents Nazi material in the movement's own terms, as a record of what its adherents wrote and honored. One technical caution: this copy's text layer is scrambled by a character-substitution cipher, which limits searching and reading on screen. It is presented as an archive holding, without endorsement, for historians of the period.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DukeStevenB_Duk:
Steven Duke wrote on April 2, 1969 to Richard G. Kleindienst, the Deputy Attorney General of the United States. Duke protested a decision by the Justice Department to retry a man named James Miller on narcotics-conspiracy charges. He called the decision a tragic error.

A private citizen writing to the department's second-ranking official is a direct form of protest. Duke put his objection in writing, at the top of the system, where it entered the official file. The letter preserves one voice against a prosecution that its writer believed should never have been brought twice.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ModernPhotoBook:
The FBI's New York office sent this memorandum to the Director, marked for the Latent Fingerprint Section. Its subject line reads 'L/MURKIN,' the bureau's King assassination case. The memo concerns a letter dated September 26, 1967, written by Eric S. Galt to the Modern Photo Bookstore. Galt was the alias James Earl Ray used before the King shooting.

A letter from a suspect, sent to a bookstore months before the crime, was physical evidence. Fingerprints on it could tie a document to a hand. The memo, kept in New York file 44-1609, shows that work in progress. It also shows the bureau still chasing paper from 1967 while the case was being built.
govdocs-archive_org-perspectives-on-init:
René Guénon published Perspectives on Initiation in 1946, near the end of his life. Guénon founded the Traditionalist school, which held that real spiritual teaching passes through unbroken chains of initiation.

The book explains what initiation is and is not: the rites that confer it, the signs by which it is known, and the slow waking of the soul it begins. Guénon separates true initiation from clubs and ceremonies that merely copy its form. For his school, the volume is a key statement of how a seeker actually enters a tradition.
govdocs-archive_org-russian-racial-scien: Russian Racial Science, Volume 2: the volume - the made public government document, subject: government records. Held as an archive item; no stance taken, a single volume, dated entry. From the archive shelves, for readers of the literature and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-stepan-bandera-selec: Stepan Bandera: Selected Works, Volume 1 - the made public government document, subject: government records. Held as an archive item; no stance taken, a single volume, dated entry. From the archive shelves, for readers of the literature and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-the-analects-of-conf:
The Analects gathers the sayings of Confucius and his talks with students, recorded by his followers after his death in 479 BC. Presented here in English, the text comes with a learned word-list keyed to book and verse for close study.

Short exchanges carry the teaching: respect for parents, care in speech, rule by moral example rather than force, and learning as a lifelong duty. Those ideas ordered Chinese family life, education, and government for two thousand years. The Analects remains the base of Confucius's school of thought, and this edition's word-list helps readers follow key terms as they recur across the whole work.
govdocs-archive_org-the-book-of-wisdom-b: The Book of Wisdom opens with Book 1, titled The Way of the Creator. The tract sets divine wisdom against worldly folly, urging the reader toward the first and away from the second. It is a devotional work rather than a study, written to guide belief and conduct. The library holds it as a religious volume from its archive set, complete in this first book of the series.
govdocs-archive_org-the-presocratic-phil: The Presocratic Philosophers gathers the earliest Greek thinkers into one volume. It runs from the forerunners who first tried to explain the world's making through to the Sophists of Athens. Thinkers like Heraclitus and Parmenides left only fragments, quoted by later writers. A collection like this one sets those fragments in order so readers can follow the birth of philosophy itself, from water and fire to atoms and argument.
govdocs-archive_org-the-symbolism-of-fre: Freemasonic Symbolism presents Freemasonry as an initiatory institution whose real teaching stays hidden in plain sight. The exposition explains the fraternity's symbols as carriers of that teaching. Masonic signs, tools, and temple forms have drawn curious readers for three centuries. A guide like this one walks through them as a system rather than a code to crack. It serves readers of fraternal history and of the symbolic reading of ritual.
govdocs-archive_org-time-machines-norber: Norbert Jürgen Ratthofer wrote Time Machines about devices classed as stationary and non-stationary. The topic belongs to fringe science: claims that time itself can be engineered. The library holds the work as an archive item, without backing. It serves readers who collect speculative writing on time travel, where physics terms and secret-project stories tend to mix. The volume presents its claims in full for that audience.
hume-history-of-england-1860-part-b:
Part B continues David Hume's History of England in the 1860 Virtue edition, three volumes split into six parts. Hume published the history from 1754 to 1762, working backward from the Stuarts to Caesar. His aim was a full national story told with a steady, skeptical mind.

The chapters in each part march year by year through reigns, wars, and parliaments. Hume treats heroes and villains with the same level gaze, which shocked readers used to party histories. The set holds all seventy-one chapters of the complete work. Part B keeps the narrative rolling in the prose that made Hume the most read historian of his century.
jeremy-and-hamlet-a-chronicle-of-certain:
Hugh Walpole published Jeremy and Hamlet in 1923, a chronicle of a boy, a dog, and a country town. He dedicated it to his father and mother as their devoted friend and son. Jeremy is ten and a half and in the lower fourth at school. A new boy, Baltimore, expects Jeremy to shield him from bullying.

Mr. Thompson said you were to see they didn't hit me, Baltimore complains. Jeremy urges him not to call the master Mr. Thompson, since nobody does. Hamlet the dog shares Jeremy's town and school world. Walpole continues the Jeremy books with warmth and close recall.
lincoln-s-gettysburg-address-given-novem:
Abraham Lincoln delivered this address at Gettysburg on November 19, 1863. The battlefield near Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, had become a cemetery ground. Project Gutenberg first issued the text among its earliest etexts. This retranscription was officially re-released on November 19, 1993.

Lincoln opens four score and seven years before his speech. He says the brave men there consecrated the ground already. The living, he argues, must dedicate themselves to unfinished work. The short speech remains America's most famous act of public mourning. The address runs only a few hundred words in full. Gutenberg timed this re-release for the speech's 130th anniversary.
report-by-the-governor-on-a-visit-to-the:
Colonial Reports number 54 prints the Newfoundland governor's report on his visit to the Micmac Indians at Bay d'Espoir. The paper was presented to both Houses of Parliament by command of His Majesty in September 1908. His Majesty's Stationery Office in London sold it for twopence.

The report takes the form of a dispatch from Government House, St. John's, dated July 8, 1908. The governor tells the Secretary of State that he left St. John's on May 28 to visit the Micmac settlement at Bay d'Espoir. His name is not given in the opening lines shown, which begin the journey's account.
ruth-fielding-on-cliff-island-or-the-old: Alice B. Emerson wrote Ruth Fielding on Cliff Island, or The Old Hunter's Treasure Box, issued by Cupples and Leon. Emerson is named as author of Ruth Fielding of the Red Mill and Ruth Fielding at Silver Ranch. A series list follows the title page, pricing each volume at forty cents, postpaid. The list runs from Ruth Fielding of the Red Mill, or Jasper Parloe's Secret, through At Briarwood Hall, At Snow Camp, and At Lighthouse Point. It ends with At Silver Ranch and On Cliff Island itself.
the-cruise-of-the-jasper-b: Don Marquis dedicates The Cruise of the Jasper B. to all copyreaders on all newspapers of America. Its contents list twenty-seven chapters. Their titles are jaunty: A Schooner, a Skipper, and a Skull; Lady Agatha's Story; First Blood for Cleggett; and more. Chapter I, A Bright Blade Leaps from a Rusty Scabbard, begins on an evening in April of a year given as 191-, with Clement J. Cleggett entering. Only the title page, contents, and the opening line are present here.
the-most-ancient-lives-of-saint-patrick-:
Title page and dedication only are present here for The Most Ancient Lives of Saint Patrick, edited with a preface and chronological table by the Rev. James O'Leary. P. J. Kenedy published the fifth edition at New York in 1880, with copyright entered in 1874. No life of the saint appears in these pages.

The title promises the life by Jocelin, hitherto unpublished in America, together with Patrick's extant writings. A frontispiece shows Saints Columba, Patrick, and Brigid, taken from a 1629 Paris engraving by Messingham. O'Leary dedicates the volume to T. W. Croke, Bishop of Auckland in New Zealand, hoping that Croke might one day be counted a St. Patrick for New Zealand.
the-parables-of-the-saviour-the-good-chi: The Parables of the Saviour, in easy verse, is the tenth book of The Good Child's Library, dated 1851, with illuminations from original designs. Only the preface and the series list are present here, so the verses themselves do not appear. The preface says the library aims to encourage a taste for Scripture reading in children. Its pictures, printed in oil colours at great expense, illustrate each history, and twelve books make up the set.
the-seminole-indians-of-florida-fifth-an: Clay MacCauley wrote The Seminole Indians of Florida for the Smithsonian Institution's Bureau of Ethnology. The report forms part of the Bureau's fifth annual report. Its pages shown here give a letter of transmittal and a detailed contents list. No report text itself follows. Chapter one treats personal characteristics, MacCauley's list says. Physique of the men and women, clothing, and personal adornment are covered. Hairdressing, beads, silver disks, and ear rings each get entries. Psychical characteristics and intellectual ability close the chapter. The next chapter begins beyond the portion shown.
theatrum-chemicum-zetzner-1602-b:
A companion gathering from Zetzner's Strasbourg press in 1602 adds more tracts to the Theatrum Chemicum. Lazarus Zetzner kept collecting the chief writers on alchemy in Latin. Together with the first gathering, it helped form one shared canon for the art.

More treatises on the great work fill these pages, in the same grand format. Readers meet famed adepts, their symbols, their furnaces, and their claims. The set gave scattered texts a stable home in print. Anyone who owned both printings held the core library of early modern alchemy, the books that serious students reached for first.
types-of-children-s-literature-a-collect:
Walter Barnes collected and edited Types of Children's Literature for use in colleges, normal schools, and library schools. A publisher's statement frames the aim: direction for parents and teachers choosing from the world's best literature for children. The domain, it says, is vast, rich, and varied.

Barnes's preface explains that the anthology grew from his own classes in children's literature. Students need specimens at hand if they are to know authors, periods, and types by study rather than hearsay. One volume of prose and poetry samples serves both class analysis and children's reading. The book treats children's literature as a field with types worth teaching, not a shelf of accidents.
un-ga-res-49-236-b:
Native peoples won a named place in Guatemala's peace under a deal marked in Resolution 49/236 B. On 31 March 1995, the state and the rebel URNG signed the Agreement on Identity and Rights of Indigenous Peoples. The vote recalls the chain of texts that set up the UN rights mission in Guatemala in 1994, and stretched its term by six months that March.

The mission chief's second report lies before the Assembly. Its counsel, sent to both the state and the URNG, weighs how each kept its pledges under the rights deal. The text takes note of that counsel in full. The native deal, with the rights mission to check it, formed one pillar of the peace that ended the war in 1996.
un-ga-res-51-198-b:
Guatemala's peace deals needed a UN watch, and Resolution 51/198 B keeps that watch in place. The Mission for the Verification of Human Rights in Guatemala had been set up in 1994. In December 1996, the government and the rebel URNG signed a firm and lasting peace at Guatemala City. The vote stretches the mission's mandate for one year, to 31 March 1998, in a fresh form fit for peace.

The text recalls the chain of votes that built the mission, from 1990 on. The Secretary-General was asked to counsel how the mission's shape and staff should change for its new task. That task: check that the pledges of the peace, on rights and far more, were kept in daily life.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 49/236 B, adopted on 14 September 1995, renewed the Guatemala human rights verification mission for six months, until 18 March 1996. The Assembly stressed the weight of the Agreement on Identity and Rights of Indigenous Peoples, signed by the parties on 31 March 1995. It called it a landmark in the International Decade of the World's Indigenous People.

The parties were told to carry out the mission director's advice from his first and second reports. They were told to keep their human rights promises, now including the indigenous peoples agreement's rights parts. The text also urges agreement on land and economic questions, the next item in the talks, toward an early final peace.

General Assembly Resolution 51/198 B, adopted on 27 March 1997, reshaped the United Nations presence in Guatemala after peace. The final peace accord of 29 December 1996 had ended the long internal conflict. Work was under way on checking the ceasefire, pulling forces apart, and disarming and demobilizing fighters. Military observers attached to the mission watched that work.

The Assembly renamed the human rights mission the United Nations Verification Mission in Guatemala. It renewed it for one year, until 31 March 1998, to verify all the peace accords. Both parties were praised for their steady search for peace and called on to keep every promise they had made.
when-knighthood-was-in-flower-or-the-lov: Only the title pages are present here for When Knighthood Was in Flower, so the tale itself does not appear. Edwin Caskoden, the pen name of Charles Major, rewrote the love story of Charles Brandon and Mary Tudor in modern English. Mary was the sister of King Henry the Eighth. The book claims to rest on a memoir by Sir Edwin Caskoden. This Julia Marlowe edition adds scenes from the play. Bowen-Merrill of Indianapolis printed it, with copyright dates of 1898 and 1901.
william-harvey-and-the-discovery-of-the-:
Thomas H. Huxley gave a lecture on William Harvey and the discovery of the circulation of the blood. Harvey, born in 1578, lived to 1657, nearly eighty years old. He was the eldest son of a small Kent landowner who sent him to Cambridge. His brothers went into trade and grew rich.

Harvey then studied at Padua in Italy, under the famed Fabricius of Aquapendente. Back in London he joined the College of Physicians and rose fast in practice. By about 1616 the college made him its professor of anatomy. Huxley traces how Harvey's work in that post led to his great find on the blood's circuit. Science and one man's patience fill the talk.
